newsitem.title: UK: Funds run the slide rule over strippable UK gilts.
newsitem.headline: Funds run the slide rule over strippable UK gilts.

text.p: Fund managers are casting a careful eye over British government bonds that will become strippable and like what they see, dealers said.
Two weeks ago, the Bank of England announced that dividends paid on strippable gilts on or after June 7, 1997 will be paid gross, with tax only payable on an annual basis by those liable to UK tax.
After weighing up the pros and cons, fund managers have snapped up those stocks to which the new arrangement applies, dealers said.
"There's been a lot of switching into those stocks on which dividends will be tax free," said a senior salesman at a UK brokerage. "These have been genuine portfolio moves in some size," he added.

Strippable gilts are bonds that can have the coupon, or annual interest payment, stripped from the bond and traded as a separate instrument. The Bank said strippable gilts will be available from early next year.
The first stocks to become strippable are the 8.0 percent gilts due 2000, the 8.5 percent gilts of 2005, the 7.5 percents of 2006, the 8.0 percent gilts due 2015 and the 8.0 percents due 2021.
The Bank said those bonds will be "gross paying", ie not subject to withholding tax. Tax will be accounted for on an annual basis for those who have to pay UK tax.
The salesman said the key thing for institutional investors was that tax payments can now be deferred.
"Funds can keep and invest all that tax income for months. Previously, tax was paid on a rolling basis," he said.

Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, said for each coupon payment on a gilt, the investor will have the use of funds representing withholding tax at 20 percent for an average of 14 months before the tax has to be paid.
The value generated by reinvesting the deferred tax payments over that period should be reflected by higher prices in the gilts involved.
But there is a caveat, he said. About half the gilt market is held by investors who already receive interest gross, such as pension funds and pension fund money managed by long-term life insurers.
Nonetheless, Adams saw particular value in long-dated strippable gilts, most notably the 8.0 percent gilt due 2015.

"At the longer end of the curve, the market does not seem to be fully valuing the benefits of gross payment. Arguably, as the actual start of the strips market draws nearer, that value will start to be recognised," he said.
The new tax arrangements could also lure in more overseas investors who, up to now, have had to declare themselves if they wished dividends to be paid gross.
"The Bank of England appears to have said dividends will now be paid gross full-stop," said one gilts analyst. "We inferred from that that overseas funds will no longer have to declare themselves."
He said mutual funds, in particular, were often not keen to name all their members.
"That could well bring more people into the market and have a small beneficial impact on those stocks," he said.
But both he and Adams said the premium for strippable gilts, because of the new tax situation, would be minor.
"Most of this information was known already," Adams said.
